---
title: "Bias from Confounding"
subtitle: "Turn the confounder up from zero and watch truth and estimate separate"
categories: [explorable, bias, confounding]
---

[Chapter 1](/notes/01-introduction.qmd) shows two points: confounding present,
confounding absent. The interesting part is the transition between them.

Two of the sliders here do completely different jobs, and telling them apart is
the whole exercise. **Confounder strength** moves the number the naive
estimator converges to. **Sample size** moves nothing except how far one study
is likely to land from that number.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false

// Same palette as the build-time charts and the site CSS.
palette = FileAttachment("../theme/palette.json").json()

// Explorables render client-side, so unlike baked charts they can simply
// react to the theme instead of being recolored after the fact.
mode = Generators.observe((notify) => {
  const read = () =>
    notify(document.body.classList.contains("quarto-dark") ? "dark" : "light");
  read();
  const obs = new MutationObserver(read);
  obs.observe(document.body, { attributes: true, attributeFilter: ["class"] });
  return () => obs.disconnect();
})

colors = ({
  control: palette.series[mode][palette.semantic.control.slot],
  treated: palette.series[mode][palette.semantic.treated.slot],
  naive: palette.series[mode][palette.semantic.naive.slot],
  truth: palette.reference[mode].truth,
  ink: palette.chrome[mode].ink,
  ink2: palette.chrome[mode]["ink-2"],
  muted: palette.chrome[mode]["ink-muted"],
  grid: palette.chrome[mode].grid,
  surface: palette.chrome[mode].surface
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false

// Deterministic RNG so a given slider position always yields the same
// picture — a chart that reshuffles on every redraw teaches nothing.
function makeRng(seed) {
  let s = seed >>> 0;
  return () => {
    s = (s * 1664525 + 1013904223) >>> 0;
    return s / 4294967296;
  };
}

// Box-Muller, standard normal.
function makeNormal(rng) {
  return () => {
    const u = Math.max(rng(), 1e-12);
    const v = rng();
    return Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(u)) * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * v);
  };
}

// The JS mirror of pylib/dgp.py confounded(): x drives both the probability of
// treatment and the outcome.
function simulate({ n, confounding, ate, seed = 42, baseline = 10, noise = 1 }) {
  const rng = makeRng(seed);
  const normal = makeNormal(rng);
  const rows = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    const x = normal();
    const p = 1 / (1 + Math.exp(-confounding * x));
    const t = rng() < p ? 1 : 0;
    const y0 = baseline + confounding * x + noise * normal();
    const y1 = y0 + ate;
    rows.push({ x, t, y0, y1, y: t === 1 ? y1 : y0, group: t === 1 ? "Treated" : "Control" });
  }
  return rows;
}

function naiveDiff(rows) {
  const t = rows.filter((r) => r.t === 1);
  const c = rows.filter((r) => r.t === 0);
  if (!t.length || !c.length) return NaN;
  return d3.mean(t, (r) => r.y) - d3.mean(c, (r) => r.y);
}

// One repetition of the whole study, keeping only the two group means.
// Materialising 100 x 5000 rows to end up with 100 numbers is what would make
// the sliders stutter.
function naiveDiffOnce(n, confounding, ate, seed, baseline = 10, noise = 1) {
  const rng = makeRng(seed);
  let spare = null;
  const normal = () => {
    if (spare !== null) { const v = spare; spare = null; return v; }
    const r = Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(Math.max(rng(), 1e-12)));
    const a = 2 * Math.PI * rng();
    spare = r * Math.sin(a);
    return r * Math.cos(a);
  };
  let s1 = 0, n1 = 0, s0 = 0, n0 = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    const x = normal();
    const t = rng() < 1 / (1 + Math.exp(-confounding * x)) ? 1 : 0;
    const y = baseline + confounding * x + noise * normal() + (t === 1 ? ate : 0);
    if (t === 1) { s1 += y; n1++; } else { s0 += y; n0++; }
  }
  return n1 && n0 ? s1 / n1 - s0 / n0 : NaN;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false

// The bias has a closed form, so it never has to be guessed from a finite
// sample — which is exactly the confusion this page exists to remove.
//
//   naive estimand = ATE + c * ( E[x | T=1] - E[x | T=0] )
//
// sigmoid(cx) is symmetric about x = 0 and x is standard normal, so
// P(T = 1) = 1/2 exactly and the bracket collapses to 4 * E[x * sigmoid(cx)],
// a single integral against the normal density. Checked against a 200,000-row
// Monte Carlo run of pylib/dgp.py confounded(): agrees to three decimals.
biasGrid = d3.range(-8, 8.0001, 0.01)
biasDensity = biasGrid.map((g) => Math.exp((-g * g) / 2) / Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI))

function biasAnalytic(c) {
  let acc = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < biasGrid.length; i++) {
    const g = biasGrid[i];
    const edge = i === 0 || i === biasGrid.length - 1 ? 0.5 : 1;
    acc += (edge * g * biasDensity[i]) / (1 + Math.exp(-c * g));
  }
  return 4 * c * acc * 0.01;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false

viewof confounding = Inputs.range([0, 4], {
  value: 1.5, step: 0.1, label: "Confounder strength"
})

viewof sampleSize = Inputs.range([200, 5000], {
  value: 1500, step: 100, label: "Sample size"
})

viewof trueAte = Inputs.range([0, 5], {
  value: 2, step: 0.25, label: "True ATE"
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false

data = simulate({ n: sampleSize, confounding, ate: trueAte })
estimate = naiveDiff(data)

// The systematic part: what the naive estimator converges to as n grows, minus
// the truth. Note what it is not a function of — the sample size.
biasTrue = biasAnalytic(confounding)
estimand = trueAte + biasTrue

// The sampling distribution. Each replicate repeats the entire study at the
// current settings. This is where the sample size does its work, and it works
// on the spread, never on the centre.
REPLICATIONS = 100
replicates = d3
  .range(REPLICATIONS)
  .map((r) => naiveDiffOnce(sampleSize, confounding, trueAte, 7919 * (r + 1)))
  .filter(Number.isFinite)

spread = d3.deviation(replicates)

// Half-width of the sampling window below. Sized from the spread at the
// SMALLEST n the slider allows, which makes it a constant with respect to n:
// the cloud can never overflow the frame, and the frame never rescales as the
// cloud shrinks. Sizing it from the current spread would hide the shrinking,
// and a flat constant would clip the cloud at n = 200.
sampMargin = Math.max(
  0.3,
  3.2 * d3.deviation(
    d3.range(REPLICATIONS)
      .map((r) => naiveDiffOnce(200, confounding, trueAte, 7919 * (r + 1)))
      .filter(Number.isFinite)
  )
)

// Analytic rather than simulated, so the curve is smooth and visibly
// unaffected by the sample-size slider. A Monte-Carlo curve would wobble
// whenever n moved, which is the very thing being disproved here.
biasCurve = d3.range(0, 4.05, 0.05).map((c) => ({
  confounding: c,
  estimand: trueAte + biasAnalytic(c)
}))
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false

scatter = Plot.plot({
  width: 700,
  height: 320,
  marginLeft: 48,
  marginBottom: 40,
  style: { background: "transparent", color: colors.ink2, fontSize: "12px" },
  x: { label: "Confounder x →", grid: true },
  y: { label: "↑ Observed outcome y", grid: true },
  color: {
    domain: ["Control", "Treated"],
    range: [colors.control, colors.treated],
    legend: true
  },
  marks: [
    Plot.dot(data, {
      x: "x",
      y: "y",
      fill: "group",
      fillOpacity: 0.4,
      r: 2.4,
      tip: true,
      title: (d) =>
        `${d.group}\nx = ${d.x.toFixed(2)}\ny = ${d.y.toFixed(2)}`
    }),
    Plot.ruleY([0], { stroke: colors.grid })
  ]
})

biasPlot = Plot.plot({
  width: 700,
  height: 250,
  marginLeft: 48,
  marginBottom: 40,
  style: { background: "transparent", color: colors.ink2, fontSize: "12px" },
  x: { label: "Confounder strength →", domain: [0, 4], grid: true },
  // The y domain always includes the truth line plus headroom for its label,
  // so the label never lands on the axis no matter where the slider sits.
  y: {
    label: "↑ What the naive estimator converges to",
    grid: true,
    domain: [Math.min(0, trueAte - 1), Math.max(...biasCurve.map((d) => d.estimand)) + 1]
  },
  marks: [
    // Truth is a reference line in chrome ink, not a competing series.
    Plot.ruleY([trueAte], { stroke: colors.truth, strokeDasharray: "3,3" }),
    Plot.text([`True ATE = ${trueAte}`], {
      frameAnchor: "top-right", dx: -6, dy: 6,
      fill: colors.truth, fontSize: 11
    }),
    Plot.line(biasCurve, {
      x: "confounding", y: "estimand", stroke: colors.naive, strokeWidth: 2
    }),
    // Where the slider currently sits.
    Plot.dot([{ confounding, estimand }], {
      x: "confounding", y: "estimand",
      r: 5, fill: colors.naive, stroke: colors.surface, strokeWidth: 2
    })
  ]
})

// A window of fixed width around the two reference lines: it reacts to the
// bias but NOT to n. That is deliberate — on an auto-scaled axis the cloud
// would always fill the frame and the shrinking would be invisible.
sampWindow = ({
  lo: Math.min(trueAte, estimand) - sampMargin,
  hi: Math.max(trueAte, estimand) + sampMargin
})

samplingPlot = Plot.plot({
  width: 700,
  height: 200,
  marginLeft: 48,
  marginRight: 20,
  marginTop: 30,
  marginBottom: 42,
  style: { background: "transparent", color: colors.ink2, fontSize: "12px" },
  x: {
    label: `${REPLICATIONS} repeats of the same study, n = ${sampleSize} each →`,
    domain: [sampWindow.lo, sampWindow.hi],
    grid: true
  },
  y: { axis: null, domain: [0, 1] },
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([trueAte], { stroke: colors.truth, strokeDasharray: "3,3" }),
    Plot.text([{ x: trueAte, y: 1, t: `truth = ${trueAte}` }], {
      x: "x", y: "y", text: "t", dy: -8,
      fill: colors.truth, fontSize: 11, textAnchor: "middle"
    }),
    Plot.ruleX([estimand], { stroke: colors.naive, strokeWidth: 2 }),
    // Inside the frame rather than under it: with no confounding the two rules
    // coincide, and a label below the frame lands on the axis ticks.
    Plot.text([{ x: estimand, y: 1, t: `converges to ${estimand.toFixed(2)}` }], {
      x: "x", y: "y", text: "t", dy: 10,
      fill: colors.naive, fontSize: 11, textAnchor: "middle"
    }),
    // One dot per repeat of the study. Jitter is derived from the index rather
    // than drawn, so the strip does not reshuffle on every redraw.
    Plot.dot(replicates, {
      x: (d) => d,
      y: (d, i) => 0.2 + 0.6 * (((i * 2654435761) % 997) / 997),
      r: 3.2, fill: colors.naive, fillOpacity: 0.42
    })
  ]
})

fmt = (v) => (Number.isFinite(v) ? v.toFixed(2) : "—")

html`<div class="explorable">
  <div class="controls">
    ${viewof confounding}
    ${viewof sampleSize}
    ${viewof trueAte}
  </div>
  <div class="plot">${scatter}</div>
  <div class="readout">
    <div>
      <span class="stat-label">True ATE</span>
      <span class="stat-value">${fmt(trueAte)}</span>
    </div>
    <div>
      <span class="stat-label">This sample's estimate</span>
      <span class="stat-value">${fmt(estimate)}</span>
    </div>
    <div>
      <span class="stat-label">Bias — set by the design</span>
      <span class="stat-value" style="color:${
        Math.abs(biasTrue) < 0.05 ? palette.status.good : palette.status.critical
      }">${fmt(biasTrue)}</span>
    </div>
    <div>
      <span class="stat-label">Spread — set by n</span>
      <span class="stat-value">± ${fmt(spread)}</span>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="plot">${biasPlot}</div>
  <div class="plot">${samplingPlot}</div>
</div>`
```

## What to notice

**Move the sample size with the confounder held high.** In the bottom strip the
cloud of repeated studies tightens, while the line it tightens *onto* does not
budge. The readout says the same thing twice: **spread** falls, **bias** does
not change at all. More data buys precision, never correctness.

**Now set the confounder to 0.** Bias becomes exactly zero and the cloud
centres on the truth. Raise the sample size from here and a single estimate
does creep toward the true ATE — but that is the spread collapsing, not a bias
being cured. There was no bias to cure.

That distinction is the thing to carry away, because a real study only ever
shows you one dot:

$$
\underbrace{\hat\tau - \tau}_{\text{how far one study lands}}
\;=\; \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\hat\tau] - \tau}_{\text{bias — the design}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\hat\tau - \mathbb{E}[\hat\tau]}_{\text{noise — the sample size}}
$$

Only the second term shrinks with $n$. So watching one estimate settle down as
data accumulates says nothing about whether it is settling on the right number.

**Change the true ATE.** The whole curve shifts vertically, but its shape is
unchanged. Bias is a property of the design, not of the size of the effect you
are hunting.

::: {.recall}
A single estimate misses the truth by **bias plus noise**, and only noise
shrinks with the sample size. An estimate stabilising as data accumulates is
therefore no evidence that it is stabilising on the truth: a biased estimator
converges too — neatly, confidently, and onto the wrong number.
:::

::: {.recall}
Bias from confounding is a property of the assignment mechanism. It survives
any sample size, and it does not depend on how large the true effect is. Only
a change in the design — or an assumption that substitutes for one — removes
it.
:::

::: {.quiz question="With the confounder at zero the bias readout stays at 0.00, yet a single estimate still misses the true ATE — and misses by less as n grows. Is that bias?"}
No, it is noise. At strength 0 assignment is a fair coin that knows nothing
about the potential outcomes, so $\mathbb{E}[\hat\tau] = \tau$ exactly: the
estimator is unbiased, and the dashed truth line runs through the middle of the
cloud at *every* sample size.

What shrinks is the width of that cloud, at rate $1/\sqrt{n}$. Bias is a
statement about where the cloud is centred; the sample size only controls how
tightly it is packed.

The trap is that a real study gives you one dot and no truth line, so from
inside it the two are indistinguishable. Telling them apart is always a claim
about the design, never a reading off the data.
:::

::: {.quiz question="The bias curve starts flat, bends sharply upward, then straightens out. Does it level off if you push the confounder far enough?"}
No — it keeps climbing, and asymptotically in a straight line. Worth being
precise about, because the curve *looks* like it is heading for a plateau.

One slider is driving two channels at once. It sets how strongly $x$ selects
who gets treated, and it also sets how strongly $x$ moves the outcome, since
$y_0 = 10 + c\,x + \varepsilon$. The selection channel genuinely does saturate:
past a certain strength nearly every high-$x$ unit is already treated and
nearly every low-$x$ unit already is not, so the gap
$\mathbb{E}[x \mid T=1] - \mathbb{E}[x \mid T=0]$ tops out at
$4\varphi(0) \approx 1.60$. The outcome channel never saturates, so the product

$$\text{bias} = c \cdot \big(\mathbb{E}[x \mid T=1] - \mathbb{E}[x \mid T=0]\big)$$

grows without bound — quadratically near zero, then linearly with slope
$\approx 1.60$.

The lesson is about the model rather than the world: when one knob drives two
mechanisms, the shape of the resulting curve belongs to neither of them.
:::
